q: How does the lecture classify a decision tree as a learning method?
choices: Non-parametric supervised learning, for classification and regression
Parametric supervised learning, for classification only
Non-parametric unsupervised learning, for clustering
Parametric supervised learning, for regression only
why: Slide 6: a decision tree is a non-parametric supervised approach used for both classification and regression.

q: Which decision-tree algorithm picks splits using entropy?
choices: ID3
CART
K-Means
Naive Bayes
why: Slide 8: ID3 measures how mixed the data is at a node with entropy. CART uses Gini impurity.

q: What does C4.5 add over ID3, according to the slides?
choices: It handles missing data and continuous attributes
It replaces entropy with the Gini impurity
It grows many trees and takes a majority vote
It can only produce binary splits on categorical data
why: Slide 8: C4.5 is an improved ID3 that can handle missing data and continuous attributes.

q: Which impurity measure does CART use, and which tasks can it do?
choices: Gini impurity; classification and regression
Entropy; classification only
Gini impurity; classification only
Information gain; regression only
why: Slide 8: CART uses Gini impurity and works for both classification and regression.

q: What is a leaf (terminal) node?
choices: A node where no further splitting happens; it gives the final outcome
The first node, where the whole dataset starts to split
Any node created by splitting the root, holding an intermediate condition
A node that has been removed by pruning to prevent overfitting
why: Slide 11: leaf nodes cannot be split further and carry the final classification; they are also called terminal nodes.

q: What is the root node of a decision tree?
choices: The top node holding the entire dataset, where splitting starts
The bottom node that outputs the final class label
The node with the highest entropy after splitting
A sub-section of the tree, like a sub-graph
why: Slide 10: the root node is where the entire population starts dividing based on features.

q: What do the slides call nodes produced by splitting the root that hold intermediate conditions?
choices: Decision nodes
Leaf nodes
Terminal nodes
Support vectors
why: Slide 10: nodes resulting from splitting root nodes are decision nodes; they represent intermediate decisions.

q: What is pruning in a decision tree?
choices: Removing nodes to prevent overfitting and simplify the model
Adding nodes until every leaf is 100% pure
Choosing the feature with the highest information gain
Sampling rows with replacement to build several trees
why: Slide 12: pruning removes or cuts down specific nodes to prevent overfitting and simplify the model.

q: According to the slides, how do decision trees fight overfitting?
choices: Pruning and setting appropriate stopping criteria
Feature scaling and one-hot encoding
Adding more depth until every node is pure
Using a larger value of the hyperparameter C
why: Slide 19: trees overfit when they capture noise; pruning and appropriate stopping criteria address this.

q: In a tree, a node that is divided into sub-nodes is called the ___, and the sub-nodes are ___.
choices: parent node; child nodes
leaf node; root nodes
child node; parent nodes
root node; support nodes
why: Slide 13: a node divided into sub-nodes is the parent; the sub-nodes emerging from it are the children.

q: How is a decision tree built, step by step?
choices: Start at the root, ask the best question, split, repeat until leaves
Start at the leaves and merge nodes until one root remains
Pick k centroids, assign points, recompute, repeat
Fit one hyperplane with maximum margin, then add kernels
why: Slide 15: start at the root, find the feature that best splits the data, branch, and repeat until reaching leaf nodes.

q: Why may a decision tree not be the globally optimal tree?
choices: It is built top-down and greedily, choosing the best split at each node only
It uses random subsets of features at every split
Entropy is always 1 at the root, so the first split is random
It needs feature scaling and the slides skip that step
why: Slide 18: trees use a top-down greedy approach maximising IG at the current node, which may not give the globally optimal tree.

q: Slide 17 says decision trees 'assume feature independence'. Which model actually makes that assumption?
choices: Naive Bayes
Decision tree
Random forest
Support vector machine
why: Feature independence is the Naive Bayes assumption. Trees split on one feature at a time and naturally model interactions; even slide 17 admits they work with correlated features.

q: Slide 20 suggests trees weight features equally 'unless feature scaling' is applied. What is actually true?
choices: Trees are invariant to feature scaling; a threshold split ignores units
Trees need min-max scaling or the largest feature dominates
Trees need standardization because entropy uses the mean
Trees only work after every feature is one-hot encoded
why: A split like 'income > 50k' picks the same rows whatever the units, so scaling does not change a tree. SVMs and KNN need scaling; trees do not.

q: Slide 16 says trees 'typically make binary splits', yet the Play-Tennis tree splits Outlook three ways. Which statement reconciles this?
choices: ID3/C4.5 allow multi-way splits; CART (and sklearn) uses binary splits
The Play-Tennis tree is wrong; Outlook must be split in two
Multi-way splits are only allowed for numeric features
All decision-tree algorithms use three-way splits at the root
why: ID3 splits a categorical attribute into one branch per value (Sunny/Overcast/Rain). CART-style trees, including sklearn's, are binary only.

q: What does the lecture say about decision trees and sample size?
choices: Small datasets may overfit; large ones may give overly complex trees
Trees need at least 1000 samples or entropy is undefined
Sample size has no effect because trees are non-parametric
Large datasets always give shallower, simpler trees
why: Slide 20: small datasets may lead to overfitting and large datasets to overly complex trees; balance sample size and depth.

q: When is a node turned into a leaf during tree building?
choices: When it is pure (100% one class)
When its entropy equals 1
When it holds more than half of the data
When its information gain is negative
why: Slide 25: we keep splitting, and when the purity is 100% we make it a leaf node.

q: What does entropy measure at a decision-tree node?
choices: Impurity: how mixed (random) the class labels are
The depth of the node from the root
The distance between the two closest points
How many features remain unused
why: Slide 24: entropy measures the impurity of a node, the degree of randomness in the data.

q: Which is the entropy formula on slide 22 (two classes)?
choices: E(S) = −p₊ log p₊ − p₋ log p₋
E(S) = 1 − p₊² − p₋²
E(S) = p₊ log p₊ + p₋ log p₋
E(S) = −log(p₊ · p₋)
why: E(S) = −p(+)log p(+) − p(−)log p(−). The log is base 2 (the slide omits it). 1 − Σp² is Gini, not entropy.

q: Entropy of a pure node, e.g. 4 Yes / 0 No?
why: p₊ = 1, p₋ = 0: −1·log₂1 − 0 = 0. A pure node has no uncertainty.

q: Entropy of a 50/50 node, e.g. 3 Yes / 3 No (log base 2)?
why: −0.5·log₂0.5 − 0.5·log₂0.5 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1, the maximum for two classes. (0.693 would be the natural-log answer.)

q: Play-Tennis root: 9 Yes, 5 No. What is E(S)?
Entropy of a node with 2 Yes / 3 No (e.g. Outlook = Sunny)?
why: −0.4·log₂0.4 − 0.6·log₂0.6 = 0.529 + 0.442 ≈ 0.971. Rain (3 Yes / 2 No) has the same entropy.

q: Slide 26: the node has 5 yes / 2 no. Its entropy is closest to:
why: −(5/7)log₂(5/7) − (2/7)log₂(2/7) ≈ 0.347 + 0.516 ≈ 0.86. The slide prints 0.85 because it rounds 2/7 to 0.28.

q: Slide 27: the node has 3 yes / 2 no. Its entropy is closest to:
why: −0.6·log₂0.6 − 0.4·log₂0.4 ≈ 0.442 + 0.529 = 0.971. The slide prints 0.966 because it rounds log₂0.6 to −0.73.

q: On slides 24–28 the left child is 5 yes / 2 no and the right is 3 yes / 2 no. Which is purer?
choices: Left: lower entropy (≈0.86 vs ≈0.97)
Right: lower entropy (≈0.86 vs ≈0.97)
Both equal, since each still has 2 no
Neither: both have entropy 1
why: Slide 28: the left node has lower entropy, i.e. more purity, so it is easier to decide there.

q: Fill in: the higher the entropy, the ___ the purity and the ___ the impurity.
choices: lower; higher
higher; lower
higher; higher
lower; lower
why: Slide 28: higher entropy means lower purity and higher impurity.

q: Entropy of a node with 1 Yes / 3 No?
Why is the entropy of a 50/50 two-class node exactly 1 and not 0.693?
choices: Decision-tree entropy uses log base 2
Entropy is divided by the number of classes
The formula squares the probabilities
Entropy is rounded up for balanced nodes
why: With log₂, −2·0.5·log₂0.5 = 1. With natural log you'd get ln 2 ≈ 0.693. The slide omits the base, but its worked numbers use log₂.

q: Gini impurity (CART) is written in the notes as:
choices: G = 1 − Σ pᵢ²
G = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ
G = Σ pᵢ²
G = 1 − max pᵢ
why: The summary gives G = 1 − Σpᵢ²; the slides name Gini (CART) but do not work it through. −Σp log p is entropy.

q: Gini impurity of a 50/50 two-class node?
why: 1 − (0.5² + 0.5²) = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5. Gini's maximum for two classes is 0.5, while entropy's is 1.

q: What does information gain tell you?
choices: How much the parent's entropy drops after splitting on a feature
How pure a single node is, on a 0–1 scale
How many leaves the final tree will have
The probability that a test point is classified correctly
why: Slide 29: information gain tells how much the parent entropy has decreased after splitting with some feature.

q: Which formula is information gain IG(S, a)?
choices: E(S) − Σᵥ (|Sᵥ|/|S|)·E(Sᵥ)
E(S) + Σᵥ (|Sᵥ|/|S|)·E(Sᵥ)
Σᵥ E(Sᵥ) − E(S)
E(S) − Σᵥ E(Sᵥ)
why: Slide 31: parent entropy minus the size-weighted average of child entropies. Forgetting the |Sᵥ|/|S| weights is the classic mistake.

q: ID3 chooses which attribute for a node?
choices: The one with the largest information gain
The one with the largest weighted child entropy
The one with the most distinct values
The one with the smallest information gain
why: Slide 31: IG decides which attribute becomes the decision or root node; the largest drop in entropy wins.

q: Parent: 4 Yes / 4 No. A split gives children 4 Yes / 0 No and 0 Yes / 4 No. Information gain?
why: E(parent) = 1. Both children are pure (E = 0), so the weighted child entropy is 0 and IG = 1 − 0 = 1.

q: Parent: 4 Yes / 4 No. A split gives two children of 2 Yes / 2 No each. Information gain?
why: E(parent) = 1 and each child is still 50/50 (E = 1), so the weighted average is 1 and IG = 1 − 1 = 0. A useless split.

q: Parent: 4 Yes / 4 No. Children: 3 Yes / 1 No and 1 Yes / 3 No. Information gain?
why: Each child has E ≈ 0.811 and holds half the rows, so the weighted entropy is 0.811. IG = 1 − 0.811 ≈ 0.189.

q: A student computes IG = E(S) − ΣE(Sᵥ) without the |Sᵥ|/|S| weights. What goes wrong?
choices: Child entropies are summed, not averaged, so IG is too small (even negative)
Nothing; the weights always add up to 1 so they cancel
IG becomes too large because the weights shrink each term
The parent entropy is counted twice
why: With two impure children the unweighted sum can exceed E(S), giving a negative 'gain'. Each child's entropy must be weighted by its share of the rows.

q: Slide 24: parent 8 yes / 4 no. What is its entropy?
In the Play-Tennis data (14 days), how many days are Yes and how many are No?
choices: 9 Yes, 5 No
5 Yes, 9 No
7 Yes, 7 No
10 Yes, 4 No
why: Slide 32's table has 9 Yes and 5 No, which is why the root shows Yes=9, No=5.

q: Outlook splits the 14 days into Sunny (2Y/3N), Overcast (4Y/0N), Rain (3Y/2N). Weighted child entropy?
Information gain of Outlook at the Play-Tennis root?
why: IG = 0.940 − 0.694 ≈ 0.247, the largest of the four attributes, so Outlook becomes the root.

q: Information gain of Humidity at the root (High 3Y/4N, Normal 6Y/1N)?
Information gain of Wind at the root (Weak 6Y/2N, Strong 3Y/3N)?
Rank the root information gains in Play Tennis, highest first.
choices: Outlook > Humidity > Wind > Temp
Humidity > Outlook > Temp > Wind
Outlook > Wind > Humidity > Temp
Temp > Outlook > Humidity > Wind
why: Outlook ≈ 0.247, Humidity ≈ 0.151, Wind ≈ 0.048, Temp ≈ 0.029.

q: Why is Overcast a leaf right after the first split?
choices: All 4 Overcast days are Yes, so its entropy is 0
Overcast has the most days of the three branches
Overcast has the highest information gain
Temperature is always Hot on overcast days
why: Overcast → 4 Yes / 0 No is pure (E = 0), so it becomes the leaf 'Yes'.

q: Which attribute splits the Sunny branch (2 Yes / 3 No) in the slide-34 tree?
choices: Humidity
Wind
Temperature
Outlook again
why: Sunny splits on Humidity: High → 0Y/3N (No), Normal → 2Y/0N (Yes). Both children are pure.

q: Which attribute splits the Rain branch (3 Yes / 2 No) in the slide-34 tree?
choices: Wind
Humidity
Temperature
Outlook again
why: Rain splits on Wind: Strong → 0Y/2N (No), Weak → 3Y/0N (Yes).

q: In the Sunny branch, what is the information gain of Humidity?
why: E(Sunny) ≈ 0.971 and Humidity makes both children pure (High 0/3, Normal 2/0), so IG = 0.971 − 0 = 0.971, the maximum possible here.

q: Slide 34: X_test = {Outlook: Sunny, Humidity: High, Temp: Hot, Wind: Weak}. Prediction?
choices: No
Yes
Cannot tell, Temp is not in the tree
Yes, because Wind is Weak
why: Sunny → Humidity; High → leaf 0 Yes / 3 No → No. Wind is only tested in the Rain branch, and Temp never appears.

q: Using the slide-34 tree, classify {Outlook: Rain, Humidity: High, Temp: Mild, Wind: Weak}.
choices: Yes
No
Cannot tell, Humidity is High
No, because Temp is Mild
why: Rain → Wind; Weak → 3 Yes / 0 No → Yes. Humidity is only tested under Sunny.

q: Which Play-Tennis attribute never appears in the final slide-34 tree?
choices: Temperature
Humidity
Wind
Outlook
why: The tree uses Outlook, Humidity (under Sunny) and Wind (under Rain). Temp has the lowest gain and is never needed.

q: Slide 33 lists two subsets of rows. What are they?
choices: The 5 Sunny days and the 5 Rain days, split next
The training set and the test set
The Yes days and the No days
Two bootstrap samples for a random forest
why: Slide 33: the Sunny rows (D1, D2, D8, D9, D11) for the left node and the Rain rows (D4, D5, D6, D10, D14) for the right node.

q: What is a random forest?
choices: An ensemble of many decision trees whose predictions are combined
One very deep decision tree grown without pruning
A decision tree that splits on random thresholds
A kernel SVM that uses trees as its kernel
why: Slide 37: many decision trees, each seeing random parts of the data, combined by voting or averaging — an ensemble technique.

q: How does a random forest combine its trees' outputs?
choices: Majority vote for classification, average for regression
Average for classification, majority vote for regression
It keeps only the tree with the highest accuracy
It multiplies the trees' probabilities together
why: Slide 40: classification uses majority voting; regression averages the trees' predictions.

q: What is a bootstrapped dataset?
choices: Rows sampled with replacement from the original, same size
Rows sampled without replacement, half the original size
The original rows sorted by the target label
The original rows with every feature standardized
why: Slide 42: each bootstrapped dataset is drawn from the original with replacement, so some rows repeat (e.g. D5 twice) and some are missing.

q: In bootstrapped dataset 1, D5 and D7 appear twice while D4 and D11 are missing. Why?
choices: Rows are sampled with replacement
Duplicates were added to fix class imbalance
D4 and D11 were outliers removed by IQR
The table has a copy-paste error
why: Sampling with replacement naturally repeats some rows and leaves others out.

q: Besides random rows, what second kind of randomness does a random forest use?
choices: Each split looks at only a random subset of features
Each tree uses a random entropy formula
Each tree gets random class labels
Each tree is pruned to a random depth
why: Slide 39: when building each tree it picks a few features at random to decide splits, which keeps the trees different.

q: In the slide-42 example, which column is blanked out in bootstrapped dataset 1?
choices: Temp
Wind
Outlook
PlayTennis
why: Dataset 1 hides Temp (and dataset 3 hides Wind): a picture of feature randomness. Tree 1 therefore uses only Outlook, Humidity and Wind.

q: Why does a random forest overfit less than a single deep tree?
choices: Random rows and features make diverse trees, and combining them cancels errors
Each tree is trained on the full dataset with all features
It uses a soft margin with a penalty parameter C
It removes all outliers before building each tree
why: Slide 40: random data and features for each tree help avoid overfitting; combining diverse trees gives a more accurate, trustworthy prediction.

q: Slide 46: x = {Sunny, Cool, High humidity, Strong wind}. Trees 1, 2, 3 all say No. Forest output?
choices: No
Yes
A tie, so no prediction
The average, 0.5
why: Majority vote of three No's is No.

q: Three trees vote Yes, No, Yes for a test point. What does a random-forest classifier output?
choices: Yes
No
Tree 1's answer only
why: Majority voting: 2 of 3 trees say Yes.

q: Slide 44, bootstrapped dataset 2: under Temp = Mild, the High-humidity rows are D4 Yes, D8 No, D8 No, D12 Yes, D14 No. Counts?
choices: 2 Yes / 3 No
3 Yes / 2 No
3 Yes / 3 No
1 Yes / 4 No
why: Count them: Yes = D4, D12; No = D8, D8, D14. The slide's tree prints Yes=3, No=2 for this node, which is a typo (the parent Mild node, 3Y/3N, only adds up with 2Y/3N + 1Y/0N).

q: Which is NOT listed as a key feature of random forest?
choices: It needs every feature to be scaled to [0, 1] first
It shows feature importance
It works for both classification and regression
It handles big and complex data
why: Slide 48 lists: handles missing data, shows feature importance, works with big/complex data, used for different tasks. Scaling is not needed for trees.

q: Which is an assumption of random forest listed on slide 50?
choices: Enough data is needed so the trees differ and learn varied patterns
All features must be independent given the class
The data must be linearly separable
The classes must be perfectly balanced
why: Slide 50: each tree decides on its own, random parts of data are used, enough data is needed, and different predictions improve accuracy.

q: Slide 48 says random forest 'handles missing data'. What's the caveat from the notes?
choices: True for C4.5-style trees; classic sklearn random forests needed imputation
False: random forests delete every row with a missing value
Only true if the missing values are MNAR
Only true for regression, never for classification
why: The summary notes that sklearn's RandomForestClassifier needed imputation until v1.4, so don't take the slide literally for sklearn.

q: Main difference between logistic regression and SVM, per the lecture?
choices: LR is probabilistic; SVM is a geometric, margin-based approach
LR is geometric; SVM is a probabilistic approach
LR is unsupervised; SVM is supervised
LR uses kernels; SVM cannot use kernels
why: Slide 4: both find a hyperplane, but LR is probabilistic while SVM is geometric and margin-based.

q: Among all hyperplanes that separate the classes, which does SVM pick?
choices: The one with the maximum margin to the nearest points of both classes
The one passing through the class means
The one that minimises the sum of squared errors
The first one found by gradient descent
why: Slides 4 and 13: SVM picks the hyperplane with the maximum distance from both classes.

q: What does the lecture advise trying first on a new classification problem?
choices: Logistic regression, then an SVM without a kernel
An RBF-kernel SVM, then logistic regression
A random forest, then a sigmoid-kernel SVM
A polynomial-kernel SVM of degree 5
why: Slide 5: first try logistic regression; if accuracy is poor, try SVM without any kernel. The two perform similarly.

q: What are support vectors?
choices: The training points closest to the hyperplane, which define it
The vectors w and b that describe the hyperplane
All misclassified training points
The points farthest from the decision boundary
why: Slide 9: support vectors are the points closest to the hyperplane; the separating line is defined with their help.

q: Which points does the SVM decision boundary depend on, versus logistic regression?
choices: SVM: only the support vectors; LR: all the points
SVM: all the points; LR: only the support vectors
Both use only the points closest to the boundary
Both use only the misclassified points
why: Slide 11: SVM is defined by the support vectors only; logistic regression's classifier is defined over all points.

q: When does the lecture say a plain linear SVM can be used?
choices: When the data is perfectly linearly separable
When the data forms concentric circles
Only when there are more than 2 features
Only when the classes are imbalanced
why: Slide 7: linear SVM when data is perfectly linearly separable; otherwise non-linear SVM with the kernel trick.

q: What is the margin in an SVM?
choices: The distance between the hyperplane and the closest points (support vectors)
The number of misclassified training points
The angle between w and the x-axis
The value of the bias b
why: Slide 9: the margin is the distance between the hyperplane and the observations closest to it; a large margin is considered good.

q: What is the equation of the SVM hyperplane and what is w?
choices: w·x + b = 0; w is normal (perpendicular) to the hyperplane
w·x + b = 1; w lies along the hyperplane
w·x − b = 2; w is the margin width
w·x = 0; w is a support vector
why: Slide 24: hyperplane w·x + b = 0, where w is a vector normal to the hyperplane and b is an offset.

q: With w perpendicular to the boundary at distance c, a point X is classified positive when:
choices: X·w > c
X·w = c
X·w < c
X·w = 0
why: Slide 21: X·w = c on the boundary, > c positive, < c negative. Replacing −c by b gives the w·x + b ≥ 0 rule.

q: The SVM decision rule from slide 25 is:
choices: y = +1 if w·x + b ≥ 0, otherwise −1
y = +1 if w·x + b ≥ 1, otherwise 0
y = +1 if w·x ≥ b, otherwise +1
y = sigmoid(w·x + b) rounded
why: Slide 25: putting −c as b, predict +1 if X·w + b ≥ 0 and −1 if X·w + b < 0.

q: w = (2, −1), b = −1. Classify x = (2, 1) with the SVM decision rule.
choices: On the boundary
why: w·x = 4 − 1 = 3; 3 + (−1) = 2 ≥ 0 → +1. In fact 2 ≥ 1, so it also sits outside the margin.

q: In the derivation, the two margin lines L1 and L2 are:
choices: w·x + b = +1 and w·x + b = −1
w·x + b = 0 and w·x + b = 1
w·x = +b and w·x = −b
w·x + b = +2 and w·x + b = −2
why: Slide 26: assume L1 is w·x + b = 1 and L2 is w·x + b = −1; the hyperplane w·x + b = 0 sits between them.

q: The two hard-margin constraints are combined into one. Which?
choices: yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1
yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≤ −1
w·xᵢ + b ≥ yᵢ
yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) = 0
why: Slides 28–29: green points need w·x + b ≥ 1, red points ≤ −1. With y = ±1 both become yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1.

q: A point has y = −1 and w·x + b = −0.5. Does it meet the hard-margin constraint?
choices: No: y(w·x + b) = 0.5 < 1, it is inside the margin
Yes: it is on the correct (negative) side
No: it is misclassified on the positive side
why: −1 × −0.5 = 0.5. It is correctly classified (negative side) but inside the margin, so the constraint ≥ 1 fails.

q: What is the SVM margin width d in terms of w?
why: Slide 35: projecting (x₂ − x₁) on w/‖w‖ and using w·x = ±1 − b gives d = 2/‖w‖.

q: If w = (3, 4), what is the margin width 2/‖w‖?
Why is maximising 2/‖w‖ written as minimising ½‖w‖²?
choices: Both are smallest-‖w‖ problems; the squared form is easier to minimise
Because ½‖w‖² equals the number of support vectors
Because the margin must be negative for minimisation
They are different problems; slide 36 is a mistake
why: Maximising 2/‖w‖ means making ‖w‖ small; minimising ½‖w‖² does the same and is a smooth cost. Slide 39 also notes max f = min 1/f.

q: Why do we divide w by ‖w‖ when projecting (x₂ − x₁) onto it?
choices: A projection needs a unit vector so only the direction counts
To make the margin equal to 1
To turn the dot product into a cross product
To guarantee w passes through the origin
why: Slides 18 and 32: to get just the projection, use the unit vector of w (magnitude 1), i.e. w/‖w‖.

q: Why does the SVM derivation use a vector w perpendicular to the boundary?
choices: It gives one standard direction to project every point and compare distances
Because w must always be the largest support vector
Because the boundary passes through the origin
So that the dot product returns a vector, not a scalar
why: Slide 22: there are infinitely many points on the boundary to measure from, so we take the perpendicular as a reference and project all points on it.

q: What does the dot product of two vectors return?
choices: A scalar: |A||B|cos θ
A vector perpendicular to both
A unit vector along A
The angle θ between them
why: Slides 15–17: the dot product gives a scalar, A·B = |A||B|cos θ; the cross product gives a vector.

q: What is the hard-margin SVM's big limitation?
choices: It only works when the data is perfectly linearly separable
It cannot be written as an optimisation problem
It always uses an RBF kernel
It ignores the support vectors
why: Slide 37: real data is hardly ever perfectly separable, so the hard-margin condition fails; soft margin fixes this.

q: What does a soft-margin SVM change?
choices: It allows a few misclassifications, paying a penalty for each
It forces every point to lie exactly on the margin lines
It removes the bias term b
It maximises ‖w‖ instead of minimising it
why: Slide 39: modify the objective so that it allows a few points to be wrongly classified.

q: The soft-margin objective on slide 40 is:
choices: J = ½‖w‖² + C Σ max(0, 1 − yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b))
J = ½‖w‖² − C Σ max(0, 1 − yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b))
J = C‖w‖² + Σ (yᵢ − wᵀxᵢ − b)²
J = ½‖w‖² + C Σ log(1 + e^(−yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b)))
why: Slide 40: the margin term plus C times the sum of hinge losses. The log term would be logistic loss.

q: Hinge loss max(0, 1 − y·f(x)) for y = +1 and f(x) = 0.5?
why: 1 − 1·0.5 = 0.5 > 0. Correct side but inside the margin, so it pays a small penalty.

q: Hinge loss for y = +1 and f(x) = 2?
why: 1 − 2 = −1, and max(0, −1) = 0. Outside the margin on the correct side costs nothing.

q: Hinge loss for y = −1 and f(x) = 0.5?
why: 1 − (−1)(0.5) = 1.5. The point is on the wrong side, so the loss is above 1.

q: What is zeta (ζᵢ) for a correctly classified point outside the margin?
choices: C
Its distance to the hyperplane
why: Slide 42: for correctly classified points zeta = 0; for wrongly classified ones it is the distance from the correct margin line.

q: Large C in a soft-margin SVM leads to:

Wider margin, more violations, smoother boundary
No change; C only affects training speed
A hard limit on the number of support vectors

q: Small C in a soft-margin SVM leads to:

Narrower margin, fewer violations, wigglier boundary
A hard-margin SVM
An error unless the data is linearly separable

q: As C → ∞, the soft-margin SVM behaves like:
choices: A hard-margin SVM (no violations tolerated)
A logistic regression
A model with the widest possible margin
A random forest of linear stumps
why: Infinite C makes any hinge loss infinitely expensive, so the solution must satisfy yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 for all points.

q: In the from-scratch SVM notebook, why are labels converted from {0, 1} to {−1, +1}?
choices: The hinge loss and constraint yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 need y = ±1
sklearn crashes on zero labels
To balance the two classes
So the accuracy score can be computed
why: The notebook comment: converting to {−1, +1} is required for SVM hinge loss; the derivation assumes y = −1 and +1.

q: Slide 49 claims 'SVM is not sensitive to outliers'. What's the fair correction?
choices: Hard-margin SVM is very sensitive; soft margin with moderate C is more robust
It is true for every SVM regardless of C
SVMs are only sensitive to outliers in the test set
Only kernel SVMs are sensitive; linear SVMs never are
why: A single outlier can become a support vector or make the hard-margin problem infeasible. The soft margin limits its influence.

q: What does the kernel trick do?

Removes features until the data is linearly separable
Replaces the hinge loss with squared error
Shrinks the data into a lower-dimensional space

There are too many points for a linear SVM
The classes are imbalanced
The features need standardizing first
why: Slide 45: we cannot draw a single line, so convert the lower-dimensional space into a higher one where a decision boundary divides the points.

By the class balance

q: x = (1, 2), z = (3, −1). Compute the polynomial kernel (xᵀz + 1)².
x = (1, 2), z = (3, −1). Compute (xᵀz)² and the explicit φ(x)·φ(z) with φ(x) = (x₁², √2x₁x₂, x₂²).
choices: Both equal 1
4 and 1
Both equal 4
1 and 9

Depends on ‖x‖

Every training point becomes a support vector
Training is impossible without a hard margin
